units.en: Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, a Carthaginian.
If it is true — and no one doubts it —
that the Roman people surpassed every nation in courage,
then it cannot be denied that Hannibal outstripped every other commander in skill by just as great a margin
as the Roman people exceed all nations in bravery.
For as often as he engaged with the Romans in Italy,
he always came away the victor.
And had he not been weakened at home by the jealousy of his own countrymen,
he seems to have been able to defeat the Romans.
But the resentment of the many overpowered the courage of one man.
Yet he kept alive the hatred of his father towards the Romans, handed down to him almost as an inheritance,
so faithfully that he laid down his life sooner than he laid down that hatred;
indeed, even once he had been driven from his homeland and depended on the resources of others,
he never once stopped waging war on Rome, at least in spirit.
For, to pass over Philip, whom Hannibal turned into Rome's enemy from a distance,
King Antiochus was, in those days, the most powerful ruler of all.
Hannibal inflamed him with so great a desire for war
that he attempted to bring his forces against Italy all the way from the Red Sea.
When Roman envoys came to Antiochus's court
to sound out his intentions and to work through secret schemes
to make the king suspicious of Hannibal,
as though he had been bribed by them and now thought differently than before —
and their scheme did not fail, and Hannibal found out about it,
and realised he was being shut out of the king's inner counsels —
he went to the king as soon as the chance arose,
and after reminding him at length of his loyalty and his hatred of Rome,
he added this: 'My father
Hamilcar,' he said, 'when I was a small boy, no more than nine years old,
as he was setting out from Carthage for Spain as commander-in-chief,
offered sacrifice to Jupiter, greatest and best of the gods.'
'While that sacred rite was being carried out, he asked me whether I wanted to go with him to the camp.
When I gladly agreed and began to beg him not to hesitate to take me, he said,
"I will — if you give me the pledge I ask for." He then led me to the altar
where he had begun the sacrifice, and, sending everyone else away, made me hold it and swear that I would never be
a friend to Rome.
That oath, given to my father, I have kept right up to this day so completely that no one should doubt
I will remain of the same mind for whatever time is left to me.
So if you plan anything friendly towards Rome, you will not be acting unwisely if you keep it from me; but when
you prepare for war, you will only cheat yourself if you do not put me in command of it.' It was at that
age, then, as I have said, that he set out for Spain with his father.
After his death, Hasdrubal took over as commander, and Hannibal was put in charge of the whole cavalry.
When Hasdrubal too was killed, the army handed him supreme command, and this was publicly
approved once word reached Carthage.
So it was that Hannibal, not yet twenty-five, became commander, and within the next
three years subdued every people of Spain by war; he took Saguntum, an ally of Rome, by
storm, and raised three very large armies.
One of these he sent to Africa, a second he left with his brother Hasdrubal in Spain, and the third he took
with him into Italy. He crossed the Pyrenean pass, and wherever his march took him he fought every people he met,
letting no one go free unless defeated.
When he reached the Alps, which separate Italy from Gaul — mountains no army had ever crossed
before him except that of the Greek Hercules, which is why the pass is still called the Graian Pass
today — he cut down the Alpine tribes who tried to stop his crossing, opened up the terrain, built roads, and made it possible
for a fully laden elephant to travel where, before, a single unarmed man could barely crawl. By this route
he brought his forces across and reached Italy.
He had already fought the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio at the Rhone and driven him back; with this
same man he fought again at Clastidium on the Po, and sent him off wounded and routed.
A third time this same Scipio, now with his colleague Tiberius Longus, met him at the Trebia;
Hannibal engaged them both and crushed them. From there he crossed the Apennines through the territory of the Ligurians,
making for Etruria.
On this march he was struck by such a severe eye infection that afterwards he never had
the full use of his right eye again. While still suffering from this and being carried in a litter, he ambushed and destroyed the consul Gaius Flaminius
and his army at Lake Trasimene, and not long after that
the praetor Gaius Centenius, along with his picked troops holding the mountain passes.
From here he reached Apulia, where the two consuls, Gaius Terentius and Lucius Aemilius, came out to meet him.
In a single battle he put both their armies to flight, killed the consul Paulus, and several ex-consuls
besides, among them Gnaeus Servilius Geminus, who had been consul the year before.
After fighting this battle he set out for Rome, unopposed. He waited for some days in the hills near the city,
and, having camped there, was on his way back to Capua when Quintus Fabius
Maximus, the Roman dictator, blocked his path in Falernian territory.
Trapped by the narrowness of the terrain, Hannibal got his army out that night without a single loss, and tricked Fabius
— for all his skill as a commander. For, under cover of darkness, he had bundles of twigs tied to the horns
of young cattle and set alight, then sent a great many of these animals scattering across the hillside.
By presenting this sudden sight he struck such terror into the Roman army that not one man dared go beyond
the rampart.
Not many days after this, he lured Marcus Minucius Rufus — the Master of Horse, holding power equal
to the dictator's — into battle by a trick, and routed him. He destroyed Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus,
consul for the second time, by luring him into an ambush in Lucania while Hannibal himself was elsewhere, and killed Marcus Claudius Marcellus,
five times consul, near Venusia in much the same way.
It would take too long to list every battle. So this one fact will be enough to show
how great a man he was: as long as he remained in Italy, no one stood against him in open battle, and no one
pitched camp against him in the open field after Cannae.
From here, still undefeated, he was called home to defend his own country, and made war against Publius Scipio, the son of the man
whom he himself had already routed first at the Rhone, again at the Po, and a third time at the Trebia.
With his homeland's resources by now exhausted, he wanted to settle the war with him for the time being, so as
to fight again later from a stronger position. A meeting took place, but no terms were agreed.
A few days after that meeting he fought this same Scipio at Zama. Beaten there, he covered — incredible as it sounds —
the distance to Hadrumetum, some three hundred miles
from Zama, in two days and two nights.
During this retreat the Numidians who had left the battlefield alongside him ambushed him; not only
did he escape them, he overpowered them in turn. At Hadrumetum he gathered the survivors of the retreat, and within a few
days, through fresh recruitment, had assembled a large force once more.
While he was throwing himself into these preparations, the Carthaginians made peace with Rome.
He nonetheless remained in command of the army afterwards and carried on operations in Africa, as did
his brother Mago, right up until the consulship of Publius Sulpicius and Gaius Aurelius.
For in their term of office, Carthaginian envoys came to Rome to thank the senate and people
of Rome for making peace with them, and to present them with a golden crown for it,
while also asking that their hostages might live at Fregellae, and that their prisoners be returned.
The senate's reply was this: their gift was welcome and accepted; the hostages
could stay wherever they had requested; but the prisoners would not be returned, because the Carthaginians still kept Hannibal — the man responsible
for starting the war, and Rome's bitterest enemy — in command of
an army, along with his brother Mago.
Once the Carthaginians learned of this reply, they recalled Hannibal and Mago home. As soon as he
returned, Hannibal was made “king” (that is, suffete), in the twenty-second year after he had first become general. For just as Rome
elected consuls, so Carthage elected a pair of kings every year.
In that office Hannibal applied himself with exactly the same energy he had shown in war.
For, through new revenues, he made sure there was not only enough money to pay what was owed to Rome under the treaty, but
also a surplus left over to store in the treasury.
Then, in the consulship of Marcus Claudius and Lucius Furius, envoys came from Rome to Carthage.
Believing they had been sent to demand his surrender, Hannibal boarded a ship in secret, before they could even be granted an audience with the senate,
and fled to Syria and King Antiochus.
Once this became known, the Carthaginians sent two ships to arrest him if they could catch him,
confiscated his property, tore his house down to its foundations,
and declared him an exile.
In the third year after fleeing his home, in the consulship of Lucius Cornelius and Quintus Minucius,
Hannibal reached Africa with five ships, in the territory of Cyrene, to see whether he might draw the Carthaginians into
Antiochus's war by holding out the promise of his support — Antiochus he had already persuaded to invade
Italy with his forces. He summoned his brother Mago to join him there.
As soon as the Carthaginians learned of this, they punished Mago in his absence exactly as they had punished Hannibal.
Their situation now hopeless, the two brothers set sail, and Hannibal reached
Antiochus. Two different accounts survive of Mago's death: some record that he died in a shipwreck, others that he was killed
by his own slaves.
As for Antiochus, if he had been as willing to follow Hannibal's advice in fighting the war as he had been in undertaking it,
he would have fought for supreme power nearer the Tiber than at Thermopylae. Yet even when
he could see the king pursuing many foolish schemes, Hannibal never once abandoned him.
He commanded a few ships, which he had been ordered to bring from Syria to Asia, and with these he fought
the fleet of Rhodes in the Pamphylian Sea. In that battle, though his side was beaten by the greater numbers of the enemy,
on the wing where he himself fought, he came out on top.
Once Antiochus had been defeated, Hannibal, fearing he might be handed over — which would certainly have happened had he ever put himself in Roman hands —
came to the Gortynians in Crete, to consider from there where he might go next.
But this shrewdest of all men could see he would be in great danger, unless he took precautions,
because of the Cretans' greed: he was carrying a large sum of money with him, and he knew
word of it had already spread.
So he devised the following plan. He filled several jars with lead and covered the tops with gold and
silver. These he deposited, in front of the leading citizens, in the temple of Diana, pretending he was entrusting his fortune
to their good faith. With them thoroughly deceived, he then filled bronze statues he had been carrying with him with all his
actual money, and left these lying casually in the open courtyard of his house.
The people of Gortyn guarded the temple with great care — not so much against anyone else as against Hannibal himself,
in case he should try to remove his own property without their knowledge and take it away with him.
Having saved his fortune in this way, and having made fools of every Cretan, Hannibal reached
King Prusias in Pontus. At his court he kept exactly the same attitude towards Italy, and did nothing else but arm and
train the king against Rome.
Seeing that Prusias lacked the resources to stand on his own, Hannibal won over other kings to his side
and drew warlike nations into alliance with him. Eumenes, king of Pergamum, a close ally of Rome,
was at odds with Prusias, and war was being fought between them on both land and sea;
but on both fronts Eumenes had the advantage, thanks to his alliance with Rome. This only made Hannibal
more determined to see him crushed — if he could remove Eumenes, he reasoned, everything else would come more easily.
To kill him, he devised the following plan.
Within a few days the two sides were due to fight it out at sea. Hannibal was outnumbered in ships, and would have to fight
by trickery, since he could not match his enemy in strength. He ordered as many live venomous snakes as possible
to be gathered and packed into earthenware pots.
Once he had collected a great number of these, on the very day set for the naval battle,
he called his marines together and gave the order: all of them were to converge on the one ship carrying King Eumenes,
while against everyone else they need only defend themselves: thanks to the great number of snakes, he told them, they would easily
manage this.
He would make sure they knew which ship the king himself was sailing on; if they either captured or
killed him, he promised they would be richly rewarded.
With his men encouraged in this way, the two fleets moved out to fight. Once the battle lines
were drawn up, and before the signal for battle was given, Hannibal, wanting his own side to know exactly where
Eumenes was, sent a messenger out in a small boat carrying a herald's staff.
When the man reached the enemy ships and, holding up a letter, announced that he was looking
for the king, he was taken straight to Eumenes, since no one doubted the letter contained some offer
of peace. Once the messenger had pointed out the commander's ship to his own side, he returned the way he had come.
But when Eumenes opened the letter, he found nothing in it except words meant to mock him.
Though he was baffled by this and could find no explanation for it, he still did not hesitate to
join battle at once.
As the two sides clashed, the Bithynians, on Hannibal's orders, all together attacked Eumenes's ship.
Unable to withstand their assault, the king sought safety in flight, and would not have escaped
had he not taken shelter within his own defences, positioned on the nearby shore.
As the other Pergamene ships were pressing their opponents harder, the earthenware pots I mentioned
earlier suddenly started being hurled onto their ships. At first these missiles only drew laughter from the fighting men,
who could not work out why this was being done.
But once they saw their ships filling with snakes, they were thrown into total panic at this new form of attack, and,
unable to tell which danger to avoid, they turned their ships around and fled back
to their own naval camp.
In this way Hannibal defeated the Pergamene fleet through strategy — and not only on this occasion, but often on other occasions too,
he drove back his enemies on land with the same cunning.
While these events were unfolding in Asia, it happened by chance that envoys of Prusias were dining in Rome with
the ex-consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus, and when Hannibal's name came up in conversation, one of them mentioned
that he was living in Prusias's kingdom.
Flamininus reported this to the senate the next day. The senators, who felt they would never be free
of plots as long as Hannibal lived, sent envoys to Bithynia — Flamininus among them —
to ask the king not to keep Rome's bitterest enemy at his court, but to hand him over. Prusias did not dare
refuse them outright,
but he did object to one thing: they should not demand that he himself do something that was against the laws of hospitality. Let them arrest him themselves, he said, if they could;
they would easily find the place where he was. For Hannibal stayed in
one place, in a fortress that the king had given him as a gift, which he had built in such a way
that he had exits on every side of the building, clearly afraid that what actually happened might come about.
When the Roman envoys reached the place and surrounded his house with a large body of troops, a boy
watching from the doorway told Hannibal that an unusual number of armed men were appearing. Hannibal
ordered him to go around every door of the building and quickly report back whether it was surrounded
on every side in the same way.
When the boy had quickly reported what the situation was and shown that every exit was blocked, Hannibal realised
this had not happened by chance, but that he himself was the target, and that he should no longer keep his life. So as not to lose it
at the will of another, and mindful of his past courage, he took the poison he always kept
with him.
So this bravest of men, after enduring so many different hardships, found peace at last in his seventieth year.
Under which consuls he died is a matter of dispute: Atticus, in his own Annals, records his death under
the consulship of Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Quintus Fabius Labeo; Polybius, under Lucius Aemilius Paulus
and Gnaeus Baebius Tamphilus; Sulpicius Blitho, under Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The Life opens like an entry in a list: name, father, nation. Naming Hamilcar at once prepares for the inherited hatred of Rome that runs through the whole Life.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: His nationality is the last word of the opening sentence, so the reader is reminded straight away that this is Rome's great enemy.

notes.label: Parenthesis
notes.body: Nepos breaks into his own sentence to insist that Rome's superiority is beyond question, which reassures his Roman readers before he praises Hannibal.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Rome is said to surpass not some peoples but all of them, which sets the highest possible standard for the comparison that follows.

notes.label: Litotes
notes.body: A double negative, "must not be denied", makes the praise of Hannibal sound reluctant but undeniable, as if the facts force Nepos to admit it.

notes.quote: tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes
notes.label: Parallelism
notes.body: The two halves of the comparison are built to match, tanto ... quanto, so Hannibal is ranked among generals exactly as high as Rome is ranked among nations.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: Hannibal excels in prudentia, intelligence and judgement, and Rome in fortitudo, courage. Nepos gives each side a different virtue, so he can praise Hannibal without making him braver than the Romans.

notes.label: Variatio
notes.body: The same idea is repeated in different words (superarit / antecedat, virtute / fortitudine), which keeps the long comparison from sounding repetitive.

notes.label: Emphatic adverb
notes.body: Two sweeping words leave no room for exceptions: Hannibal won every time he met the Romans in Italy, which is a strong claim to put to a Roman audience.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The sentence ends on "the winner", so the reader is left with the image of Hannibal coming away victorious.

notes.quote: nisi … debilitatus esset … videtur superare potuisse
notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: The past unreal condition imagines a Carthaginian victory, and the cautious videtur ("he seems") softens a claim that might shock Roman readers.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Hannibal is beaten by his own people, not by Rome, which makes him a tragic figure betrayed by those who should have supported him.

notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: Many are set against one, and spiteful criticism against true courage. The sentence sums up the whole Life in a single neat contrast.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: Hatred of Rome is described as property handed down in a will, which makes it part of Hannibal's identity, something he was born into.

notes.label: Hyperbole
notes.body: Hannibal would sooner lose his life than his hatred, which stresses how completely it controls him.

notes.quote: numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis
notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: numquam closes the chapter: even as an exile with no army, Hannibal keeps fighting Rome in his mind, which prepares for the rest of the Life.

notes.label: Hamilcar
notes.body: Hamilcar Barca, Carthage's leading general in the First Punic War (264 to 241 BC), who went on to build a new Carthaginian power in Spain. He died there in 229 BC.

notes.label: Exile
notes.body: Hannibal was forced to leave Carthage in 195 BC, when his enemies there told the Romans he was plotting with Antiochus. He spent the rest of his life at the courts of foreign kings (chapters 7 to 12).

notes.label: Praeteritio
notes.body: Nepos says he will pass over Philip (Philip V, king of Macedon, who allied with Hannibal against Rome in 215 BC) yet names him all the same. This lets him slip in one more example of Hannibal turning a king against Rome without breaking off from the story of Antiochus, so the reader sees Antiochus as part of a pattern.

notes.label: Emphatic placement of absens
notes.body: absens comes straight after quem, ahead of the rest of the clause, so the stress falls on the fact that Hannibal made Philip Rome's enemy without being there in person. This shows how far his hatred could reach, since even at a distance his influence was enough to turn a king against Rome.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: Calling Antiochus (Antiochus III, ruler of the Seleucid empire, to whom Hannibal fled in 195 BC) the most powerful king of the age raises his status as high as it can go. The greater the king, the more impressive it is that Hannibal could steer him against Rome.

notes.quote: omnium iis temporibus potentissimus rex Antiochus
notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: omnium is separated from potentissimus by iis temporibus and placed first in the sentence. Opening with "of all" stresses the scale of Antiochus's power before we know who is meant, and his name is saved for the end as the climax.

notes.label: Fire metaphor
notes.body: incendit means "set on fire", so Hannibal is presented as the spark that ignites Antiochus's desire for war. Fire suits the idea because it spreads quickly and is hard to control, which suggests that once Hannibal has lit it, the king's eagerness grows far beyond where it started (as the Red Sea clause then shows). It also makes Hannibal the active force and Antiochus the one acted upon, so the drive for war against Rome clearly comes from Hannibal.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: bellandi ("of waging war") belongs with cupiditate but is held back until after the verb. This puts "war" in the final position of the clause, so it lands with extra weight and leaves no doubt about what Hannibal's influence was directed towards.

notes.label: Geographical extremes
notes.body: Nepos marks the two ends of the planned expedition, from the Red Sea at the eastern edge of Antiochus's empire all the way to Italy. Stretching the war across almost the whole known world shows how vast an undertaking Hannibal inspired, and so how powerful his hatred of Rome must be to have set it in motion.

notes.label: Final position of Italiae
notes.body: Italiae is the last word of the sentence, so the target of the whole enterprise is held back until the end. The delay builds towards Rome's homeland as the climax, making Italy feel like the destination of everything Hannibal has stirred up.

notes.quote: ad quem cum legati venissent ... tempore dato adiit ad regem
notes.label: Periodic sentence
notes.body: The sentence piles up clauses about the Roman envoys and their plot (cum ... venissent, qui ... explorarent darentque, ut ... adducerent, tamquam ... sentiret) and then Hannibal's discovery of it, and the main verb adiit only arrives at the very end. The reader is kept waiting and hemmed in, much as Hannibal is hemmed in by the scheme, so that when the main verb finally comes it shows him breaking out and acting decisively.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated hard c binds "plans" and "secret" together so that they are heard as a single idea, plotting done out of sight. By making the secrecy stand out, Nepos presents the Roman envoys as sly and underhand, which colours how the reader judges Rome in this episode.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The Romans work through secret plans, whereas Hannibal responds by openly reminding the king of his loyalty (fide). Setting Roman deceit against Hannibal's frankness makes him the more trustworthy figure, and makes his hatred of Rome seem more understandable given how the Romans behave.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The envoys aim to make Antiochus think Hannibal has been bribed (corruptus) by the Romans themselves (ab ipsis). The irony is that the only ones acting corruptly are the Romans, who are secretly deceiving the king, while the man they accuse of being bought is the one whose hatred of Rome could never be bought. ipsis sharpens this, since the accusation comes from the very people guilty of underhand dealing.

notes.label: Alliteration (minor point)
notes.body: The repeated a sound ties together "different" and "before", underlining the change of heart the Romans want Antiochus to believe in. The sound draws attention to the very lie being spread, that Hannibal is no longer the man he was.

notes.quote: neque id frustra fecissent idque Hannibal comperisset seque ... segregari vidisset
notes.label: Polysyndeton
notes.body: Three clauses are joined by repeated connectives: neque ("and ... not"), idque ("and this") and seque ("and himself"). Each connective adds a new stage (the plot works, Hannibal finds out, he sees himself shut out), and chaining them together makes the stages pile up one after another. The pressure on Hannibal builds quickly, so the reader feels his position worsening just before he acts.

notes.label: Vivid word choice
notes.body: segregari comes from se + grex and literally means "to be separated from the flock", while interioribus consiliis pictures an inner circle of advisers. Together they show Hannibal being cut off and left outside, and the passive voice stresses that this is being done to him, which makes his danger clear and explains why he must speak up.

notes.quote: de fide sua et odio in Romanos
notes.label: Pairing of key ideas
notes.body: Loyalty (fide) and hatred of Rome (odio in Romanos) are placed side by side as the two things Hannibal stresses. Linking them shows that for Hannibal they go together, since his hatred of Rome is the proof of his loyalty to Antiochus, which is exactly the argument the anecdote that follows is designed to support.

notes.label: Direct speech
notes.body: Nepos switches from reporting what Hannibal said to giving his own words. This makes the moment more vivid and dramatic, and because the story comes from Hannibal's own mouth it carries his personal authority, so the hatred is something he himself declares.

notes.label: Emphatic word order
notes.body: pater meus opens the speech, ahead even of Hamilcar's name. Putting "my father" first frames everything that follows as an inheritance, so the hatred is presented as a family duty handed down from father to son.

notes.label: Diminutive
notes.body: puerulus is a diminutive of puer, meaning "little boy". It stresses how young Hannibal was, which shows how deeply rooted his hatred is, since it was instilled before he was old enough to choose it and has shaped his whole life since.

notes.quote: utpote non amplius VIIII annos nato
notes.label: Precise detail of age
notes.body: Giving an exact age adds a specific, memorable detail that makes the story sound authentic. It also reinforces the diminutive, and non amplius ("no more than") even hints that he may have been younger, emphasising how early the hatred began.

notes.label: Solemn religious formula
notes.body: "Best and greatest" is the formal cult title of Jupiter used in official worship. Such grand, ceremonial language raises the tone and makes the scene feel sacred, so the hatred that comes out of it seems sanctioned by the gods and therefore binding.

notes.label: Ritual setting
notes.body: The sacrifice of victims creates a formal religious occasion, which prepares for the oath that follows. An oath sworn in such a setting is all the more serious, so the scene builds up the weight of the promise Hannibal is about to describe.

notes.label: Roman name for a Carthaginian god
notes.body: The god Hamilcar sacrificed to was Carthaginian (probably Baal Hammon), but Nepos gives him Jupiter's name. This makes the scene familiar to a Roman reader, who would immediately grasp how solemn and binding a sacrifice to the chief god was.

notes.label: Philip V
notes.body: Philip V, king of Macedon (221 to 179 BC). After Cannae he made an alliance with Hannibal in 215 BC, which led to the First Macedonian War with Rome. Hannibal and Philip never met, hence absens.

notes.label: Antiochus III
notes.body: Antiochus III, called the Great, ruler of the Seleucid empire from 223 to 187 BC. Hannibal joined him in 195 BC and advised him during his war with Rome (192 to 188 BC).

notes.label: The Red Sea
notes.body: For the Romans the mare rubrum could mean the waters south and east of Arabia as far as the Persian Gulf. Nepos means the far eastern edge of Antiochus' empire.

notes.label: The Roman embassy
notes.body: Livy tells of a Roman embassy to Antiochus in 193 BC, whose members met Hannibal at Ephesus and talked with him often, so that the king began to distrust him.

notes.label: Hamilcar goes to Spain
notes.body: Hamilcar left for Spain in 237 BC, after the First Punic War, to build a new power base for Carthage there. Hannibal, born in 247 BC, was nine.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Calling the sacrifice a "divine matter" reminds the reader that the oath is sworn in the presence of the gods, which makes it binding for life.

notes.label: Indirect question
notes.body: Hamilcar asks rather than orders, so the boy appears to choose his future freely.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Libenter shows the boy's eagerness: from the very beginning Hannibal wanted to be a soldier.

notes.quote: ab eo petere coepissem ne dubitaret ducere
notes.label: Role reversal
notes.body: The father makes the offer, but it is the son who ends up pleading, which shows how keen Hannibal was.

notes.quote: Faciam, inquit si mihi fidem, quam postulo, dederis
notes.label: Direct speech
notes.body: Hamilcar's words are quoted, short and conditional. The bargain is made in a single sentence, which gives it the force of a contract.

notes.label: Key word
notes.body: Fides, good faith, is exactly what Antiochus doubts. By using the word, Hannibal reminds the king that his loyalty was promised before the gods.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: Simul makes the action follow at once: there is no time for the boy to reconsider.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: Sending the others away makes the oath private and solemn, a bond between father and son alone.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The boy swears with his hand on the altar, a physical gesture that makes the scene easy to picture and the oath sacred.

notes.quote: numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore
notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: Numquam makes the oath absolute and lifelong. The phrasing is careful: he swears never to be Rome's friend, which echoes the end of chapter 1.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The oath comes first and the pronoun ego is added for emphasis, so Hannibal moves from the story to his own personal claim.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The oath has lasted from boyhood to old age, so the reader feels the length of Hannibal's commitment.

notes.quote: ita conservavi, ut nemini dubium esse debeat
notes.label: Result clause
notes.body: The result clause turns his past record into proof: if he kept the oath this long, he will keep it now.

notes.label: Litotes
notes.body: "Not unwisely" is a polite understatement. Hannibal tells the king to hide any friendliness towards Rome from him without sounding like a threat.

notes.quote: si quid amice de Romanis cogitabis … cum quidem bellum parabis
notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The two halves of his advice are set side by side: keep peace plans from him, but give him war. The balance shows that Hannibal is useful to the king only as an enemy of Rome.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Hannibal bluntly tells a king that he would be fooling himself without him, which shows his confidence in his own value.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Hannibal ends his speech by asking to be put in command, so the last word of his self-defence is a claim to leadership.

notes.quote: hac igitur, qua diximus, aetate cum patre in Hispaniam profectus est
notes.label: Ring structure
notes.body: Nepos steps back in with qua diximus and returns to Hannibal's age, rounding off the story and taking the narrative back to the start of his career.

notes.label: Spain
notes.body: Carthage had lost Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica to Rome after the First Punic War. Hamilcar's Spanish empire, with its silver mines and manpower, gave Carthage the resources for a second war.

notes.quote: cuius post obitum, Hasdrubale imperatore suffecto … hoc quoque interfecto
notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: Two ablative absolutes dispose of two commanders in a few words, hurrying the story on to the moment Hannibal takes charge.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Even before he is in overall command, Hannibal is given a major responsibility, which marks him out early.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The same verb is used for the army giving him command and the news being brought to Carthage, linking the soldiers' choice to the city's approval.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Nepos stresses that Hannibal's command was legitimate, approved by the state, not seized by force.

notes.label: Hyperbole
notes.body: Nepos claims Hannibal conquered all of Spain in three years, an exaggeration that makes his speed and success seem astonishing.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: Foederatam reminds the reader that Saguntum was Rome's ally, so the attack is an act of war on Rome itself, told in a single matter-of-fact phrase.

notes.quote: omnes gentes Hispaniae bello subegit; Saguntum … vi expugnavit, tres exercitus maximos comparavit
notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.body: Three achievements follow one another without connecting words, which gives an impression of rapid, relentless activity.

notes.quote: unum in Africam misit, alterum cum Hasdrubale fratre in Hispania reliquit, tertium in Italiam secum duxit
notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: The three armies are dealt out in three balanced clauses, and the climax is the one Hannibal leads himself.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: A strong negative with nisi leaves no exceptions: every people on the march was beaten.

notes.label: Relative clause
notes.body: Nepos explains the Alps as a natural barrier, which builds up the scale of what Hannibal is about to do.

notes.quote: nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium
notes.label: Comparison
notes.body: Hannibal's only predecessor is a legendary hero, so his crossing is placed on the level of myth.

notes.quote: concidit; loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit
notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.body: A string of short verbs with no connectives conveys the speed and energy of the work.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The huge, laden elephant is set against a lone man without even a weapon, which shows how completely Hannibal transformed the route.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Repere, "to crawl", paints the mountain path as almost impassable before Hannibal's engineers arrived.

notes.quote: hac copias traduxit in Italiamque pervenit
notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: After the long description, the arrival is told in a few quick words, so the chapter ends on Hannibal in Italy.

notes.label: Hasdrubal
notes.body: Hamilcar's son-in-law, who commanded in Spain from 229/8 BC until he was murdered in 221 BC. Not to be confused with Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal (unit 7).

notes.label: Saguntum
notes.body: A city on the east coast of Spain, south of the Ebro, on friendly terms with Rome. Hannibal's siege of it in 219 BC led directly to the Second Punic War.

notes.label: Hasdrubal, Hannibal's brother
notes.body: He held Spain for Carthage until 208 BC, then led an army into Italy to reinforce Hannibal, but was defeated and killed at the Metaurus in 207 BC.

notes.label: Hercules and the Alps
notes.body: Legend said that Hercules had crossed the Alps on his way back from Spain with the cattle of Geryon. The name of the Graian Alps (the area of the Little St Bernard Pass) was linked with him, though it more likely comes from a local people.

notes.label: Pluperfect
notes.body: The pluperfects reach back before chapter 3 ended, so the narrative picks up events that happened on the way to the Alps.

notes.quote: cum hoc eodem … tertio idem Scipio
notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: Nepos keeps stressing that it is the same Roman commander, beaten again and again, which makes Hannibal's dominance seem relentless.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The switch into the present makes this second battle vivid, as if happening before the reader's eyes.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Two participles show the consul both hurt and running, a humiliating picture of a Roman commander.

notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.body: Two short clauses with no connective: the battle is over as soon as it begins.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Two consuls together still cannot stop Hannibal, which raises the scale of the victory.

notes.quote: adeo gravi morbo afficitur oculorum, ut postea numquam dextro aeque bene usus sit
notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: Right in the middle of his victories, Hannibal is shown as a man suffering lasting physical harm, which makes him human.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: The great general is too ill to walk or ride, which makes what follows all the more remarkable.

notes.quote: lecticaque ferretur, C. Flaminium consulem … occidit
notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: A sick man in a litter destroys a consul and his army: the contrast shows that Hannibal's mind, not his body, wins battles.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Hannibal wins by cunning, a theme that runs through the Life: Romans fall into his traps.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Even Rome's best troops are beaten, which adds to the sense that no one can resist him.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Rome sends both its consuls at once, a sign of how desperate the situation has become.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Two consular armies routed in one battle: the phrase stresses the scale of Cannae without needing to name it.

notes.quote: Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares, in his Cn. Servilium Geminum
notes.label: Climax
notes.body: The list of dead rises from a consul to a group of ex-consuls, so the reader sees how much of Rome's leadership died at Cannae.

notes.label: Precise detail
notes.body: Naming a man who was consul only a year earlier makes the losses concrete and personal for Roman readers.

notes.label: Publius Cornelius Scipio
notes.body: Consul in 218 BC and father of Scipio Africanus, who would beat Hannibal at Zama. At the Rhône there was only a clash of cavalry patrols: Scipio arrived after Hannibal had already crossed.

notes.label: Clastidium and the Po
notes.body: The battle usually called the Ticinus (218 BC), a cavalry battle near the Po, in which Scipio was badly wounded. Clastidium was a nearby town that Hannibal later took.

notes.label: The Trebia
notes.body: A tributary of the Po. In December 218 BC Hannibal lured the Romans across the freezing river and ambushed them with troops hidden in a stream bed.

notes.label: Lake Trasimene
notes.body: In June 217 BC Hannibal trapped Flaminius' army in mist between the hills and the lake shore. Flaminius and about 15,000 Romans were killed.

notes.label: Cannae
notes.body: Cannae, in Apulia in south-east Italy, where in 216 BC Hannibal encircled and destroyed the army of Paullus and Varro (here C. Terentius).

notes.label: Figura etymologica
notes.body: The noun and the participle come from the same root, a heavy, emphatic way of marking the end of Cannae.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: Two words tell us that after Cannae there was nothing between Hannibal and Rome.

notes.quote: in propinquis urbi montibus moratus est
notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Hannibal camping within sight of Rome is a frightening image for Roman readers, and moratus est hints at a missed chance.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Fabius is given his full name and title, which builds him up as a worthy opponent before Hannibal outwits him.

notes.label: Participle
notes.body: The perfect participle shows Hannibal apparently caught, which makes his escape more striking.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: Ullo stresses that the escape was complete: not a single man was lost.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The superlative praises Fabius' cunning in the very clause where he is fooled, which makes Hannibal even cleverer. Dare verba is an idiom for deceiving someone.

notes.quote: sarmenta in cornibus iuvencorum deligata incendit
notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The precise, strange detail of burning branches on the cattle's horns lets the reader picture the trick in the dark.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: The darkness is described as a covering, which suits a trick that depends on not being seen clearly.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Numbers and scattering make the lights seem like a whole army on the move.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Repentino stresses the shock of the moment, which explains the panic that follows.

notes.quote: tantum terrorem iniecit … ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus
notes.label: Result clause
notes.body: The result clause shows the scale of the fear: a whole Roman army stays behind its wall.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Dolo again: Hannibal wins by deception, the quality Romans both feared and condemned as Punic treachery.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: The same word was used of Hannibal turning Philip against Rome (chapter 2). Hannibal can destroy his enemies even when he is not there.

notes.quote: Ti. Sempronium Gracchum, iterum consulem … M. Claudium Marcellum, quinquies consulem
notes.label: Climax
notes.body: The victims grow in seniority, ending with a man who had been consul five times, so the list builds to its most impressive name.

notes.label: Praeteritio
notes.body: Nepos says he will not list every battle, which suggests there were far too many victories to count.

notes.quote: nemo ei in acie restitit, nemo adversus eum
notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: Repeating nemo at the start of both clauses drives home the claim that no Roman could face him.

notes.label: Rhetorical emphasis
notes.body: Ille gives Hannibal a grand, almost admiring tone, and the whole sentence is built to prove his greatness.

notes.label: Capua
notes.body: The richest city of Campania, which went over to Hannibal after Cannae and served as his base. Rome besieged and retook it in 211 BC.

notes.label: The ager Falernus
notes.body: Rich farmland in northern Campania, famous for its wine. In 217 BC Fabius tried to trap Hannibal in the valley there.

notes.label: Minucius
notes.body: Fabius' Master of Horse in 217 BC. Frustrated with Fabius' caution, the people gave him equal command; he attacked Hannibal and had to be rescued by Fabius.

notes.label: Gracchus and Marcellus
notes.body: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus was killed in an ambush in Lucania in 212 BC. Marcellus, the captor of Syracuse and called the Sword of Rome, died in an ambush near Venusia in 208 BC.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The first word of the chapter: Hannibal leaves Italy unbeaten, so whatever happens at Zama, his record in Italy stands.

notes.label: Supine
notes.body: The supine expresses purpose: Hannibal is called home not to attack but to defend, which makes him a patriot.

notes.quote: primo apud Rhodanum, iterum apud Padum, tertio apud Trebiam
notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three battles, three numbered stages: the list reminds the reader of the father's defeats as the son steps forward.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: Carthage's weakness, not Hannibal's, is given as the reason he wants peace, so the blame for the defeat is moved away from him.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Even his peace offer is a military tactic: Hannibal is still planning the next war.

notes.quote: in colloquium convenit; condiciones non convenerunt
notes.label: Wordplay
notes.body: The same verb is used of the men meeting and the terms failing to meet, a neat play on words that sums up the conference.

notes.quote: in colloquium convenit; condiciones non convenerunt
notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.body: Two short clauses with no connective make the failure of the talks blunt and final.

notes.quote: apud Zamam cum eodem conflixit: pulsus
notes.label: Understatement
notes.body: The decisive defeat of the war is told in one participle, pulsus, so Nepos moves quickly away from Hannibal's only great loss.

notes.label: Narrator's comment
notes.body: Nepos steps in to marvel at the speed of the retreat, so the focus shifts from defeat to another feat of endurance.

notes.quote: biduo et duabus noctibus … milia passuum trecenta
notes.label: Precise detail
notes.body: Exact numbers make the march sound measured and real, which makes the claim more impressive.

notes.quote: qui simul cum eo ex acie excesserant, insidiati sunt ei
notes.label: Irony
notes.body: His own companions in flight turn against him, which shows how dangerous his position was after the defeat.

notes.quote: non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit
notes.label: Climax (non solum … sed etiam)
notes.body: The construction builds to a climax: escape would have been enough, but Hannibal crushes his attackers too.

notes.quote: novis dilectibus paucis diebus multos contraxit
notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Paucis and multos are set against each other: within days of a crushing defeat Hannibal has a large army again, which shows his energy and resilience.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The chapter ends on Hannibal rebuilding, not on his defeat, so the reader is left with an image of recovery.

notes.label: Scipio Africanus
notes.body: Publius Cornelius Scipio (236 to 183 BC), son of the consul of 218 BC. He drove the Carthaginians out of Spain, invaded Africa in 204 BC and defeated Hannibal at Zama, earning the name Africanus.

notes.label: Zama
notes.body: In 202 BC, south-west of Carthage. Scipio won with the help of Masinissa's Numidian cavalry, and the battle ended the Second Punic War.

notes.label: Hadrumetum
notes.body: A coastal city south of Carthage (modern Sousse in Tunisia). The real distance from Zama was well under half Nepos' three hundred miles.

notes.label: The Numidians
notes.body: The peoples west of Carthage, famous horsemen. Some fought for Carthage at Zama, others, under Masinissa, for Rome. This ambush is reported only by Nepos.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: The superlative adverb shows Hannibal throwing all his energy into preparing for more war, which makes the peace made behind his back all the more of a blow.

notes.quote: cum in apparando acerrime esset occupatus, Carthaginienses bellum cum Romanis composuerunt
notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: Hannibal's preparations for war are set against his city making peace. This is the first sign of the split between Hannibal and his own people that leads to his exile.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The phrase shows Hannibal carrying on regardless, as if the peace did not apply to him.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Mago is linked to Hannibal, so the Barca brothers act as one. This prepares for the senate naming them both in its reply.

notes.label: Roman point of view
notes.body: Nepos dates events in Carthage by the Roman consuls, so the story is told from Rome's side even when the scene is Africa.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: The envoys come to thank, to give and only then to ask. Putting the thanks and the gift first shows Carthage humbly trying to win Rome's goodwill.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: A gift of gold shows how eager the Carthaginians are to please Rome, which makes their general's continued command look like an embarrassment.

notes.quote: responsum est: munus eorum gratum acceptumque esse
notes.label: Indirect speech
notes.body: The senate's answer is reported in indirect statement, which gives it the cool, formal tone of an official decree.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two near-synonyms make the reply sound gracious, which makes the refusal that follows all the sharper.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The senate grants the first request and refuses the second. The balanced reply makes the "no" stand out.

notes.quote: Hannibalem, cuius opera susceptum bellum foret
notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Hannibal is named and blamed for starting the war in the same breath. Rome holds him personally responsible.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: The superlative and the phrase "the Roman name" make Hannibal the enemy of everything Rome stands for. This is the Roman view of him, put in the senate's own words.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Rome's complaint is that Hannibal is still in command. The word shows Roman suspicion that the war is not really over while he holds an army.

notes.label: Enclosing word order
notes.body: The Carthaginians are placed inside the ablative absolute, wrapped up in Rome's reply, which suits a city now ruled by Rome's wishes.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Carthage obeys at once and recalls its greatest general to please Rome, which foreshadows how readily it will abandon him later.

notes.quote: ut enim Romae consules, sic Carthagine … reges
notes.label: Comparison
notes.body: Nepos explains a foreign office by comparing it with a Roman one. The balanced ut … sic helps his Roman readers and makes Carthage look like a mirror of Rome.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Rex was a hated word at Rome, so calling Hannibal a "king" might startle Roman readers. Nepos explains at once that the office lasted only a year, like a consulship.

notes.label: The peace of 201 BC
notes.body: After Zama (202 BC) Carthage gave up Spain and almost all its fleet, agreed to pay 10,000 talents over fifty years, and could not make war without Rome's permission.

notes.label: Mago
notes.body: Hannibal's younger brother, who fought with him in Italy and later commanded in Spain and northern Italy. Nepos's account of Mago here and in chapter 8 does not match Livy, who says Mago died in 203 BC of a wound on the voyage home from Italy.

notes.label: Fregellae
notes.body: A Latin colony on the river Liris, south-east of Rome. Carthaginian hostages could be kept there in some comfort, away from the city.

notes.label: Suffetes
notes.body: Carthage's two chief magistrates, elected every year, were called suffetes. Hannibal held the office in 196 BC. Nepos uses the Roman word rex for it.

notes.label: Praetor
notes.body: Nepos uses a Roman title for Hannibal's command of the army in Spain, which he took over in 221 BC. Counted from then, Nepos's "twenty-second year" does not quite fit the date of his suffeteship, 196 BC.

notes.quote: pari diligentia … ac fuerat in bello
notes.label: Comparison
notes.body: Peace is measured against war: Hannibal brings to politics the same energy he brought to the battlefield, so his talents are not only military.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Diligentia means hard work and attention to detail, a quality Romans admired in a magistrate. Nepos presents Hannibal as a model official.

notes.quote: non solum ut esset pecunia … sed etiam superesset
notes.label: Climax
notes.body: Not only … but also builds to a climax: Hannibal finds enough to pay Rome and then more besides.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The same verb returns with a prefix, so the step from enough to more than enough is heard in the words themselves.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Rome's greatest enemy now uses his skill to make sure Carthage keeps up its payments to Rome.

notes.label: Juxtaposition
notes.body: The envoys are placed between the two cities' names, so the reader sees Rome reaching directly into Carthage's affairs.

notes.quote: hos Hannibal ratus sui exposcendi gratia missos
notes.label: Participle
notes.body: Ratus gives the reason as Hannibal's own belief. Nepos does not confirm it, so the reader is left to judge whether he was right.

notes.label: Gerundive
notes.body: The gerundive of purpose spells out what Hannibal fears: being handed over to Rome, the fate he spends the rest of the Life escaping.

notes.quote: priusquam iis senatus daretur, navem ascendit clam
notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: Hannibal acts before the Romans can even speak, which shows his decisiveness and his distrust of his own city.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The great general slips away in secret, a sad change from the commander of armies.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: The prefix pro- gives a sense of flight far away. It is the first of several escapes in the second half of the Life.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Nepos switches to Poeni, the usual Roman name for the Carthaginians, just as they turn on their own hero.

notes.quote: Poeni naves duas, quae eum comprehenderent, si possent consequi, miserunt
notes.label: Delay
notes.body: The verb is held back behind a purpose clause and a condition, so the hunt for Hannibal is described before we learn that the ships were actually sent.

notes.quote: miserunt, bona eius publicarunt, domum a fundamentis disiecerunt, ipsum exulem iudicarunt
notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.body: Four actions follow one another with no connecting words, which makes Carthage's response sound swift and relentless.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Destroying the house to its foundations wipes out Hannibal's place in the city, an act of hatred as much as of law.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The man who has just filled the treasury is condemned by the city he served, which shows the jealousy Nepos blamed in chapter 1.

notes.label: Hannibal's reforms
notes.body: Livy (33.46–47) says that as suffete Hannibal broke the power of the corrupt judges' council and exposed the embezzlement of public money, so that the indemnity could be paid without new taxes on ordinary citizens.

notes.label: The date
notes.body: They were consuls in 196 BC. Hannibal's flight from Carthage is usually dated to 195 BC.

notes.label: Antiochus
notes.body: Antiochus III "the Great", Seleucid king from 222 to 187 BC, ruled from Syria an empire reaching to Iran. His ambitions in Asia Minor and Greece brought him into conflict with Rome. Hannibal joined him at Ephesus in 195 BC.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: At marks a turn in the story: Carthage has condemned him, but Hannibal is back at the front of the sentence and still active.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The tiny force shows how far Hannibal has fallen, yet his aim is still to drag Carthage into a war with Rome.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two near-synonyms show the method Hannibal now relies on: persuasion, not armies.

notes.label: Pluperfect
notes.body: The pluperfect shows that Hannibal has already won Antiochus over, which stresses his influence over kings.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Italy comes near the end of the clause: Hannibal's goal has not changed since the Alps.

notes.quote: Magonem eadem, qua fratrem, absentem affecerunt poena
notes.label: Parallelism
notes.body: Carthage treats the brothers exactly alike, which shows how completely the city has turned against the Barca family.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Mago is condemned without being heard, which makes Carthage's justice look hasty and unfair.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: Two words sum up the brothers' position before they sail away.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated v sound adds weight to a poetic phrase which suggests the brothers abandoning themselves to fortune.

notes.quote: alii naufragio, alii a servulis ipsius
notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: Nepos sets out both versions side by side and does not choose, like a careful researcher.

notes.label: Diminutive
notes.body: The diminutive is contemptuous: a famous commander dies at the hands of mere slaves, a humiliating end.

notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: A past unreal condition imagines what might have been, as in chapter 1. If Antiochus had taken Hannibal's advice, the war would have been fought in Italy.

notes.quote: tam in gerendo bello … quam in suscipiendo
notes.label: Parallelism
notes.body: The matching gerunds contrast the king who took Hannibal's advice to start the war with the king who ignored it while fighting.

notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: Rome's own river is set against a pass in distant Greece, which shows how close Rome came to real danger.

notes.quote: multa stulte conari … nulla deseruit in re
notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: Many foolish schemes are set against not a single desertion, which contrasts the foolish king with his loyal adviser.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Hannibal is given only a small command, which suggests that Antiochus undervalued him.

notes.label: Echo
notes.body: Ipse stresses Hannibal's personal success in a lost battle, and superior echoes chapter 1, where he always came away the victor.

notes.label: Cyrene
notes.body: Cyrene was a Greek city in Libya, east of Carthaginian territory, a safe place from which to contact Carthage.

notes.label: Thermopylae
notes.body: The narrow pass in central Greece where Antiochus was defeated by the Romans under Manius Acilius Glabrio in 191 BC, after which he withdrew to Asia.

notes.label: The battle off Pamphylia
notes.body: The battle of the Eurymedon, off Side in southern Asia Minor, in 190 BC. Rhodes, an ally of Rome, defeated the king's fleet, though the wing Hannibal commanded held its own.

notes.label: Mago's death
notes.body: Neither of Nepos's versions matches Livy, who says Mago died in 203 BC of a wound on the way home from Italy.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: The defeat of a great king is dismissed in two words, because Nepos's interest is Hannibal, not Antiochus.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Hannibal's fear of surrender, already seen in chapter 7, drives the rest of his life.

notes.label: Authorial comment
notes.body: Nepos steps in to confirm that the danger was real, so Hannibal's flight looks prudent rather than cowardly.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: The superlative introduces a trickster story. Callidus means shrewd but also cunning, a word that fits Roman ideas about "Punic" cleverness.

notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: The condition shows Hannibal thinking ahead, the quality that saves him in the trick that follows.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The Cretans are defined by greed, so the reader enjoys seeing the greedy outwitted.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The switch to the present tense makes the trick vivid, as if we are watching Hannibal at work.

notes.quote: complet plumbo, summas operit auro et argento
notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: Worthless lead inside, precious metal on top: the whole trick is caught in one contrast.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated p sound draws attention to the witnesses, who are the very people being fooled.

notes.quote: simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere
notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Hannibal pretends to rely on fides, the honesty the Cretans lack, so the trick turns their own vice against them.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: The deception is finished in four words, and the story moves straight on to the real hiding place.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Abicit, "tosses aside", shows the real treasure left carelessly in full view, which is the cleverest part of the plan.

notes.quote: non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale
notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: The temple is guarded against its depositor, a comic reversal that shows how completely the Cretans have been fooled.

notes.quote: ne ille inscientibus iis tolleret sua
notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The Cretans guard jars of lead, while Hannibal's real wealth lies in his courtyard. Sua, "his own things", adds to the joke.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two verbs for removing the treasure show how anxiously the Cretans imagine Hannibal's escape.

notes.label: Gortyn
notes.body: Gortyn was one of the leading cities of central Crete, famous for its inscribed law code.

notes.label: Cretans
notes.body: The Cretans had a proverbial reputation for greed and dishonesty: the line "Cretans are always liars" is attributed to the Cretan poet Epimenides.

notes.label: Diana
notes.body: The temple of Artemis (Diana to the Romans). Temples were often used as safe places to deposit money and valuables.

notes.quote: sic conservatis suis rebus Poenus illusis Cretensibus omnibus
notes.label: Balance
notes.body: Two ablative absolutes frame the subject, one for his money saved and one for the Cretans fooled, so the trick is summed up neatly before the story moves on.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Nepos calls Hannibal "the Phoenician", the Roman word that brought to mind proverbial Punic cunning, just after he has tricked the Cretans.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Not some Cretans but all of them were fooled, which completes the joke of the last chapter.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: His hatred of Rome is unchanged by exile, as Nepos promised in chapter 1.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: The negative shows Hannibal's single-minded focus: everything he does at Prusias' court is aimed at Rome.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two verbs show Hannibal turning a king into a weapon against Rome, as if Prusias were one of his soldiers.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Minus, "less", gently plays down the king's weakness, but the point is clear: Prusias cannot fight Rome alone.

notes.quote: conciliabat ceteros reges, adiungebat bellicosas nationes
notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.body: Two matching clauses without a connecting word, both in the imperfect, show Hannibal's tireless diplomacy.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: Eumenes is defined by his friendship with Rome, the opposite of Hannibal, so his conflict with Prusias becomes Hannibal's war with Rome by proxy.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: The war is fought on every front, which raises the stakes.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The reason for Eumenes' advantage comes last: behind every enemy Hannibal faces, Rome is the real power.

notes.quote: quem si removisset, faciliora sibi cetera fore arbitrabatur
notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: The condition shows Hannibal's clear strategic reasoning: remove the key ally and the rest will follow.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: A violent verb shows how far Hannibal is prepared to go.

notes.label: Gerundive
notes.body: The blunt gerundive of purpose, with its old-fashioned -und- spelling, states Hannibal's aim without softening: murder.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.body: The phrase echoes capit tale consilium in the Cretan story, so the reader expects another clever trick.

notes.label: Prusias
notes.body: Prusias I, king of Bithynia (about 228 to 182 BC), in north-west Asia Minor. Nepos says Pontus, loosely: Bithynia lay on the coast of the Black Sea, the Pontus Euxinus.

notes.label: Eumenes
notes.body: Eumenes II, king of Pergamum (197 to 159 BC), Rome's loyal ally in Asia Minor, who gained much of Antiochus' former territory at the peace of Apamea and fought Prusias in the 180s BC.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The verb comes first, so Hannibal's disadvantage is stated bluntly before anything else, and the reader wonders how he can possibly win.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: dolo is placed first in its clause: since he cannot win by numbers, cunning becomes his weapon, which is the theme of the whole episode.

notes.label: Gerundive of obligation
notes.body: The impersonal gerundive presents trickery as a necessity forced on him, not a choice, which lets Nepos excuse a method that Romans might think unworthy of a soldier.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: Trickery is set against armed strength, the two ways of winning a battle. Hannibal lacks the second, so he turns to the first.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: quam with the superlative stresses the scale of the plan: Hannibal does nothing by halves.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Three words pile up the danger: they are snakes, they are venomous, and they are alive. The strange weapon would startle any reader.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Cheap clay pots that would shatter on impact: the homely detail makes the secret weapon all the more surprising.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The same word returns in different cases: Hannibal's lack of numbers in ships is answered by a multitude of snakes.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: ipso stresses the timing: the plan is revealed to the men only on the day of the battle, which keeps it secret and raises the tension.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The switch to the present tense brings the reader into the moment of Hannibal's briefing, which makes the narrative vivid.

notes.label: Juxtaposition
notes.body: "All" is set right beside "one": every Bithynian ship is to converge on a single target.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: unam is separated from navem, so the single target frames the king's name and the verb.

notes.quote: omnes … in unam … a ceteris tantum
notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The men are to throw everything at one ship and merely defend themselves against the others. The balance makes the plan easy to grasp.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Hannibal speaks with complete confidence: the snakes will "easily" do the rest. The reader sees his assurance as a commander.

notes.quote: id illos facile serpentium multitudine consecuturos
notes.label: Indirect speech
notes.body: Hannibal's orders are reported in indirect speech, so Nepos can summarise the briefing briskly without stopping the story.

notes.quote: quem si aut cepissent aut interfecissent
notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: aut … aut makes either outcome worth the reward, which shows that Hannibal wants Eumenes out of the battle whatever it takes.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: magno is separated from praemio, so the promise of a great reward stretches across the clause and ends the chapter on the men's incentive.

notes.label: Eumenes
notes.body: Eumenes II, king of Pergamum in north-west Asia Minor from 197 to 159 BC. He was Rome's most loyal ally in the region and Prusias' neighbour and enemy.

notes.label: Marines
notes.body: The soldiers carried on board ship to fight, as distinct from the rowers and sailors.

notes.label: The snakes
notes.body: The same stratagem is described by Justin (32.4), who adds that the pots were thrown onto the enemy ships, as here.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: The ablative absolute wraps up the previous scene in a few words, so the story moves straight on to the battle.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the launching of the two fleets vivid and immediate.

notes.label: Delay
notes.body: The temporal clause holds the fighting back: Hannibal's trick takes place in the tense moment before the battle begins.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: His name comes in the middle of the long sentence, after the scene is set, so attention moves from the two fleets to the one man in control.

notes.quote: ut palam faceret suis, quo loco Eumenes esset
notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.body: The purpose of the messenger is told to the reader before the enemy can guess it, so we watch the Pergamenes walk into the trap.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The tiny boat and the herald's staff make the messenger look harmless and official, which is exactly why the trick works.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The sentence ends on a crisp present-tense verb: Hannibal acts.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The letter held up for all to see is the bait: it gets the messenger taken to the king, and so reveals which ship is his.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Everyone is sure the letter is about peace, but the reader knows the plan. The same words opened the Life (1.1), where they backed a certainty that was true; here the certainty is wrong.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The messenger is taken to the king immediately, which shows how easily the trick succeeds.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: The real purpose of the mission is achieved in an ablative absolute, almost in passing, as if it were a minor detail.

notes.label: Ring structure
notes.body: The messenger returns exactly where he started, his job done, which shows how smoothly the plan unfolds.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: at marks a sharp turn from the messenger's success to the king's confusion.

notes.quote: nihil … nisi quae ad irridendum eum pertinerent
notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: The letter holds only insults: Hannibal humiliates the king even before the battle, which shows his contempt for Rome's ally.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two verbs show Eumenes puzzled and baffled, so the reader enjoys knowing what he does not.

notes.label: Litotes
notes.body: The understatement makes Eumenes seem bold, but the reader knows he is hurrying into a trap.

notes.label: The herald's staff
notes.body: The caduceus (Greek kerykeion) was the staff of heralds and envoys and the emblem of Hermes. It marked its bearer as sacred and not to be harmed, so it guaranteed the messenger safe passage.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Even in the heat of battle the Bithynians act on Hannibal's orders, which keeps him at the centre of the victory.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Every Bithynian ship attacks the king's, exactly as Hannibal ordered: the plan works to the letter.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The target and the attack end the sentence, and the historic present adoriuntur makes the onslaught vivid.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: Unable to withstand the force, the king looks for safety in flight: Rome's proud ally is reduced to running away.

notes.quote: quam consecutus non esset, nisi … se recepisset
notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: The past unreal condition shows how narrow his escape was: only his defences on the shore saved him.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The rest of the Pergamene fleet is winning, which makes the sudden reversal more striking.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: repente comes before the pots are named, so the reader feels the surprise before seeing the weapon.

notes.label: Narrator's aside
notes.body: Nepos reminds the reader of the pots from chapter 10. The reader, unlike the Pergamenes, knows what is inside them.

notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.body: The Pergamenes laugh at clay pots as weapons, but the reader knows what they hold, so the laughter is short-lived.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: "At first" signals that the mood is about to change.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: serpentibus is separated from oppletas and held back to the end of the clause, so the snakes arrive as a shock.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The prefix per- and the word nova ("unheard of") explain the panic: nothing had prepared them for this.

notes.label: Indirect question
notes.body: Snakes on board and enemies all round: the sailors cannot decide which danger is worse, which shows total confusion.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Turning the sterns is a vivid way of saying they fled, the opposite of facing the enemy.

notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: Strategy defeats weapons: two words set side by side sum up the episode.

notes.quote: neque tum solum, sed saepe alias
notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The general statement widens the episode into proof of Hannibal's genius on land as well as at sea.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: prudentia recalls chapter 1, where Hannibal surpasses all other generals in prudentia: the episode confirms Nepos' first judgement.

notes.label: Bithynians
notes.body: The subjects of Prusias, from Bithynia in north-west Asia Minor, between the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea.

notes.label: Pergamum
notes.body: From Pergamum, Eumenes' capital in north-west Asia Minor, one of the richest Hellenistic kingdoms and Rome's chief ally in the region.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The scene switches from Hannibal's victories in Asia to Rome, where his fate is about to be decided.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Nepos stresses chance: Hannibal's downfall begins with a careless remark at a dinner, not with a defeat in battle.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The relaxed setting of a dinner party contrasts with its deadly result, which makes the betrayal seem casual.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: The ablative absolute makes the mention of his name seem offhand, just a turn in the conversation.

notes.label: Ablative absolute
notes.body: Two words express the senate's view: as long as Hannibal is alive, Rome is not safe. It is a striking tribute to the fear he still inspires as an old exile.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: numquam and sine together make Rome's fear absolute.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: The superlative sums up the Roman view of Hannibal and recalls the lifelong hatred described in chapter 1.

notes.label: Litotes
notes.body: The understatement shows Prusias' weakness: the king Hannibal served is too afraid of Rome to protect him.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Prusias keeps to the letter of hospitality while betraying its spirit: he will not hand Hannibal over himself, but tells the Romans where to find him.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: facile echoes Hannibal's own confident facile in chapter 10; now the word is used against him.

notes.quote: sic aedificarat, ut in omnibus partibus aedificii exitus haberet
notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Hannibal's foresight shows in the design of his house: he has planned for exactly this danger.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.body: quod accidit tells the reader that the feared moment has come, which creates suspense before the scene itself.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The scene is seen through the eyes of a slave boy at the door, which makes Hannibal's last moments small and personal.

notes.label: Indirect question
notes.body: Hannibal's calm, practical question shows a commander still assessing his position at the very end.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: The exits he built so carefully are all blocked: the repeated word shows his precautions defeated.

notes.quote: non fortuito factum, sed se peti
notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: The story began with chance (casu) and ends with a deliberate hunt for Hannibal. He sees the truth at once.

notes.quote: neque sibi diutius vitam esse retinendam
notes.label: Gerundive
notes.body: The gerundive presents his death as a conclusion he reaches calmly, not a moment of panic.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Hannibal chooses the manner of his own death, so even in defeat he keeps control.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Nepos presents the suicide as an act worthy of his past, in keeping with the Roman ideal of a noble death.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The poison comes early in its clause and sumpsit is held to the very end, so the narrative of the Life closes on his final act.

notes.label: Prusias
notes.body: Prusias I, king of Bithynia (about 230 to 182 BC), who gave Hannibal refuge and made him a commander in his war against Eumenes of Pergamum.

notes.label: Flamininus
notes.body: Titus Quinctius Flamininus, consul in 198 BC, defeated Philip V of Macedon at Cynoscephalae in 197 and proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks in 196. He led the embassy that came for Hannibal in about 183 BC.

notes.label: Patres conscripti
notes.body: The formal title of the members of the Roman senate, literally "enrolled fathers".

notes.label: The poison
notes.body: Livy (39.51) says Hannibal had kept the poison ready for a long time against exactly this; Juvenal (Satire 10) says it was carried in a ring.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: The final verdict on Hannibal is the highest praise, given by a Roman writer to Rome's greatest enemy.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: The two adjectives sum up the long and eventful life told in the previous chapters.

notes.label: Euphemism
notes.body: Nepos calls the death a rest after hardship, a gentle word for a death by poison, which gives the Life a peaceful close.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: anno is separated from septuagesimo by the verb, so his great age is the last word of the sentence.

notes.label: Change of tone
notes.body: The story ends and the scholar takes over: Nepos turns from praise to a plain discussion of his sources.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three authorities with three different dates are listed in turn, which shows Nepos' care with sources and leaves the question open.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: at and autem mark each new disagreement, so the sources are set against one another.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Nepos cites his friend Atticus first and names his work, a mark of both friendship and respect for Atticus as a chronographer.

notes.label: His age
notes.body: Nepos' figure is too high. Hannibal was born in 247 BC, so he died in his mid-sixties.

notes.label: Dating by consuls
notes.body: M. Claudius Marcellus and Q. Fabius Labeo were consuls in 183 BC, L. Aemilius Paulus and Cn. Baebius Tamphilus in 182, and P. Cornelius Cethegus and M. Baebius Tamphilus in 181.

notes.label: Atticus
notes.body: Titus Pomponius Atticus (110 to 32 BC), Nepos' close friend and Cicero's correspondent, whose Liber Annalis was a compact chronology of Roman history. Nepos also wrote a Life of Atticus.

notes.label: Polybius
notes.body: The Greek historian (about 200 to 118 BC), brought to Rome as a hostage after 167 BC, who wrote a history of Rome's rise to power including the Hannibalic War.

notes.label: Sulpicius Blitho
notes.body: A Roman writer known only from this passage; nothing of his work survives.
